definition: How many frames a single drawn (or keyed) pose is held before the next distinct pose appears — "drawing on ones/twos/threes" in traditional terms — as a deliberate stylistic and economic choice, not merely a byproduct of frame rate.
purpose: Control whether motion reads as smooth/full or graphic/stepped ("limited") animation, and trade authoring cost against smoothness on fast or high-volume work.
visible_effect: A new distinct pose every frame (ones) reads as maximally smooth; every second frame (twos) is the traditional default and still reads as smooth at normal viewing speed; every third-or-more frame (threes+) reads as increasingly stepped/graphic ("limited") animation.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Twos are indistinguishable from ones at normal speed for most motion and read as lively rather than smoothed-out; ones can look jittery on slow actions because the precision needed between very close drawings is hard to hit, while stepped/threes+ reads as intentionally graphic or energetic on fast actions, and as cheap or robotic on slow ones.
physical_interpretation: Not physical — a sampling-rate choice for the POSE stream itself, orthogonal to the physical motion being represented.
use_cases: fast, high-energy action where a stepped/graphic feel is the intended style (anime-influenced game combat)
a slow action held on twos to avoid the jitter that can appear between very close poses drawn on ones
reducing authoring cost on high-volume secondary characters or background motion
non_use_cases: a realistic or "full" animation style aiming for maximal smoothness, where ones (or a dense, continuously-keyed curve) is the correct choice
a slow, delicate motion where a stepped hold pattern would read as choppy rather than deliberate
any phase whose `timing` aspect is locked, since changing hold density edits key placement/count, not values in place
interactions: Slow in/slow out — a DIFFERENT axis: that principle shapes the curve BETWEEN two poses, this one decides how many distinct poses exist per unit time in the first place
Timing — hold density is timing's complement: timing says how long a phase lasts, hold density says how densely it is sampled
Style — the defining visual signature of "limited" vs "full" animation styles

style_variations.anime: threes or an irregular stepped pattern on key hits is a genre-defining convention, not a limitation
style_variations.realistic: ones or a dense continuous curve is expected; visible stepping reads as a technical fault
style_variations.mechanical: even, regular stepping can suit a deliberately robotic read — the one style where stepping and this table's usual "mechanical" warning are not in tension

cadence_representation: Not represented as a deliberate dial. Cadence keys are continuous by default; `set_easing`'s stepped/constant family (named already under `slow_in_slow_out`'s cadence_representation) can hold a value between two keys, but nothing in `ai/vocabulary.js` treats hold-length-across-a-whole-phase as a style choice the way `spacing_evenness` treats curve shape — nothing plans a controlled, roughly-uniform hold pattern.
control_surface: `set_easing` per-key, manually, to a stepped style; no vocabulary dimension or planner strategy addresses hold density as a phase-wide property.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Partially measurable: key count and spacing per unit time on a track is data `ai/motion.js`/the track itself already carries (keys are timestamped), so an average "frames per distinct pose" figure over a phase is computable from existing data — but nothing in this build computes or reports it today.
generation_or_modification_methods: None. No strategy in `ai/plan.js` inserts or removes keys to change hold density (Phase 3's planner may not add or remove a key, per CLAUDE.md); a caller wanting this today would have to place stepped keys manually.
failure_modes: ones (or a dense curve) on a slow action, which can look jittery rather than smooth, because the precision needed between very close poses is hard to hit
an inconsistent hold length within one phase, which reads as an authoring accident rather than a deliberate stepped style
applying a stepped hold pattern under a realistic style, which contradicts that style's expectation of continuous smoothness
roblox_considerations: Roblox's Animation Editor and exported KeyframeSequences support stepped interpolation per key the same way Cadence does, so nothing here is Roblox-specific beyond ordinary export fidelity.
performance_implications: Fewer distinct keys per second is marginally cheaper to author and to store, though Cadence keys carry no runtime evaluation cost either way.
examples: a single lean-of-the-head example shown at 0, 1, 2, and up to 10 in-betweens, each count reading as a different action or intensity (video 1 @ 16:35–17:22)
a fast flurry of activity named as one case where drawing on ones — not twos — is necessary for the action to read at all
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/uDqjIdI4bF4 @ 16:11–18:20 — Alan Becker narrates and shows the same lean at 0–10 in-between counts, and separately states the ones/twos/threes convention and its jitter/cost tradeoffs; experimental until validated
